## This tag leaks credentials. Do not use it.

Its own release notes said "use this one". That was true of the tags before it and false of
the tags after it, and the list below is what a later audit found by building 0.4.0 and
attacking the real binary rather than reading its changelog.

**It stays resolvable on purpose.** Deleting a tag buys nothing against an attacker, since
clones, forks and cached commit views all survive it, and it breaks anyone already pinned
here. The disclosure record is the reason to trust the current release, so it is not being
quietly dropped.

**Be precise about whose credentials leaked.** The library failed to redact ITS USERS'
secrets: a credential a caller passed into `SecretRedactor.redact` could survive the
redactor and reach the model. No credential belonging to the author has ever been in this
repository, and every credential-shaped string under `Tests/` is synthetic.

## What is wrong with it, measured against a real build

- **A denylist entry written any way other than a bare host matches nothing at all.**
  `https://evil.com`, `evil.com:443`, `evil.com/path` and `*.evil.com` are all silently
  inert against your config, so your own denylist fails open while looking correct in the
  file. **This is the one to check if you have ever pinned 0.4.0.**
- **Loopback and NAT64 SSRF bypasses are allowed.** `http://127.0.0x.1/` is loopback,
  because `inet_aton` reads a bare `0x` as zero and the hex-label check required more than
  two characters. `http://127.0.0.1.nip.io/` is loopback via a wildcard resolver. NAT64
  local-use reads only the `/96` embedded-IPv4 position, so an address carrying a private
  target where RFC 6052 puts it for a `/48` or a `/64` passes with a public decoy in the
  slot the code inspects.
- **An indented PEM leaks its body verbatim.** The whole-block pattern is line-anchored
  with no tolerance for leading whitespace, so a key inside YAML, JSON, a markdown block or
  a code sample matches its header and stops. The body then depends on the entropy pass,
  which needs mixed case and a digit, so a single-case base64 line walks out underneath a
  header that has been helpfully replaced with `[REDACTED:PEM]`.
- **`PGPASSWORD=`, session cookies, `Set-Cookie`, bare `Bearer` headers and `curl -u`
  passwords all go out in full.** A session identifier is what a stolen cookie replays, and
  `Bearer <token>` with no header name in front of it is how `curl -v` and most request
  logs print it.
- **The attacker chose the audit label.** `tag` scanned the denial reason for substrings and
  the bad-scheme reason interpolates the attacker's own scheme into itself, so
  `denylist://x` reported as `USER_DENYLIST`. Anyone counting denial classes was reading
  numbers hostile input could move.
- **The fence neutralised one tag in one case.** The body could open a second block with an
  attacker-chosen `kind`, and `</UNTRUSTED_DATA>` passed through untouched.

## Correction: three defects described elsewhere never shipped in this tag

A pre-public audit checked the changelog narrative against a real 0.4.0 build and found
that three defects described in the 0.5.0 notes were introduced and fixed entirely inside
the unreleased window. A consumer pinned to 0.4.0 was never exposed to them: the quadratic
denial of service (measured at 0.007s here on the exact shape that took 11 seconds
mid-window), `curl -u` swallowing the following URL, and "most specific wins" downgrading a
Stripe key inside a `postgres://` URL. The released-version story is simpler and worse, and
it is the list above.

## What it fixed

Secrets recognised by their label rather than their length. The path heuristic that was
discarding 14% of AWS secret access keys. Private key bodies inside JSON where newlines are
escaped as `\n`. Named cloud metadata endpoints such as `metadata.google.internal` and
`kubernetes.default.svc`. Six provider patterns the generic pass structurally cannot see.
And the 0.3.1 test that pinned a leak as correct.

## What to use instead

**0.6.1**, or at minimum 0.5.0, which is the first tag with no known credential leak. Note
that the module is `GruxKit` up to and including 0.5.0 and `Grux` from 0.6.0 onward.

```swift
.package(url: "https://github.com/dotcomjack/grux.git", from: "0.6.1")
.product(name: "Grux", package: "grux")
```

## Full record

The complete narrative, including the wrong first attempts, is in
[CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/dotcomjack/grux/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). The README
section [Earlier tags leak credentials](https://github.com/dotcomjack/grux#earlier-tags-leak-credentials)
lists what each of the six leaking tags does.
